returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Photo identification requirements for federal elections (S. 5271): Requires voters to show physical photo ID to get a ballot in federal elections. Someone without ID can cast a provisional ballot, but it only counts if they show ID within three days (or swear they lack it for religious reasons). Voting by mail would require sending a copy of a photo ID, or the last four digits of a Social Security number plus a sworn statement that ID couldn't reasonably be obtained. Overseas military voters and certain disabled or elderly voters are exempt, and states must work to make free ID imaging available. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-11, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

En bloc consideration of nominations (S.Res. 817): A Senate procedure step: it lets the Senate vote on a large batch of presidential nominations all at once instead of one at a time — executive-branch officials, judges, and ambassadors, including posts at the Departments of Defense, Energy, Interior, State, and Treasury and several boards and commissions. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-03, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (S.J.Res. 181): Orders the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities in or against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending against an attack on itself, its personnel, or its facilities in other countries. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-05-06, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Photo identification requirements for federal elections (S. 5271): Requires voters to show physical photo ID to get a ballot in federal elections. Someone without ID can cast a provisional ballot, but it only counts if they show ID within three days (or swear they lack it for religious reasons). Voting by mail would require sending a copy of a photo ID, or the last four digits of a Social Security number plus a sworn statement that ID couldn't reasonably be obtained. Overseas military voters and certain disabled or elderly voters are exempt, and states must work to make free ID imaging available. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-11, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

En bloc consideration of nominations (S.Res. 817): A Senate procedure step: it lets the Senate vote on a large batch of presidential nominations all at once instead of one at a time — executive-branch officials, judges, and ambassadors, including posts at the Departments of Defense, Energy, Interior, State, and Treasury and several boards and commissions. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-03, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (S.J.Res. 181): Orders the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities in or against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending against an attack on itself, its personnel, or its facilities in other countries. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-05-06, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. The CARES Act (March 2020): The first pandemic relief law: $1,200 payments to most adults, expanded unemployment benefits, and forgivable loans to keep small businesses paying staff. The House agreed to the Senate amendment by voice vote on March 27, 2020, so there is no House roll-call position for an individual member. returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Photo identification requirements for federal elections (S. 5271): Requires voters to show physical photo ID to get a ballot in federal elections. Someone without ID can cast a provisional ballot, but it only counts if they show ID within three days (or swear they lack it for religious reasons). Voting by mail would require sending a copy of a photo ID, or the last four digits of a Social Security number plus a sworn statement that ID couldn't reasonably be obtained. Overseas military voters and certain disabled or elderly voters are exempt, and states must work to make free ID imaging available. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-11, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

En bloc consideration of nominations (S.Res. 817): A Senate procedure step: it lets the Senate vote on a large batch of presidential nominations all at once instead of one at a time — executive-branch officials, judges, and ambassadors, including posts at the Departments of Defense, Energy, Interior, State, and Treasury and several boards and commissions. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-03, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (S.J.Res. 181): Orders the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities in or against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending against an attack on itself, its personnel, or its facilities in other countries. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-05-06, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: The American Rescue Plan (March 2021): The second big pandemic package: $1,400 payments, an expanded child tax credit that paid parents monthly for a year, and money for vaccines, schools and state governments. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.

returnedRecords.text: The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (2021): About $550 billion in new money for roads, bridges, water pipes, rural broadband and the electric grid, spread over five years. returnedRecords.text: The Bipartisan Safer Communities Act (2022): The first major federal gun law in about 30 years — tougher checks for buyers under 21, money for state red-flag programs and school mental health. returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Photo identification requirements for federal elections (S. 5271): Requires voters to show physical photo ID to get a ballot in federal elections. Someone without ID can cast a provisional ballot, but it only counts if they show ID within three days (or swear they lack it for religious reasons). Voting by mail would require sending a copy of a photo ID, or the last four digits of a Social Security number plus a sworn statement that ID couldn't reasonably be obtained. Overseas military voters and certain disabled or elderly voters are exempt, and states must work to make free ID imaging available. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-11, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

En bloc consideration of nominations (S.Res. 817): A Senate procedure step: it lets the Senate vote on a large batch of presidential nominations all at once instead of one at a time — executive-branch officials, judges, and ambassadors, including posts at the Departments of Defense, Energy, Interior, State, and Treasury and several boards and commissions. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-03, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (S.J.Res. 181): Orders the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities in or against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending against an attack on itself, its personnel, or its facilities in other countries. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-05-06, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Photo identification requirements for federal elections (S. 5271): Requires voters to show physical photo ID to get a ballot in federal elections. Someone without ID can cast a provisional ballot, but it only counts if they show ID within three days (or swear they lack it for religious reasons). Voting by mail would require sending a copy of a photo ID, or the last four digits of a Social Security number plus a sworn statement that ID couldn't reasonably be obtained. Overseas military voters and certain disabled or elderly voters are exempt, and states must work to make free ID imaging available. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-11, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

En bloc consideration of nominations (S.Res. 817): A Senate procedure step: it lets the Senate vote on a large batch of presidential nominations all at once instead of one at a time — executive-branch officials, judges, and ambassadors, including posts at the Departments of Defense, Energy, Interior, State, and Treasury and several boards and commissions. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-03, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (S.J.Res. 181): Orders the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities in or against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending against an attack on itself, its personnel, or its facilities in other countries. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-05-06, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Photo identification requirements for federal elections (S. 5271): Requires voters to show physical photo ID to get a ballot in federal elections. Someone without ID can cast a provisional ballot, but it only counts if they show ID within three days (or swear they lack it for religious reasons). Voting by mail would require sending a copy of a photo ID, or the last four digits of a Social Security number plus a sworn statement that ID couldn't reasonably be obtained. Overseas military voters and certain disabled or elderly voters are exempt, and states must work to make free ID imaging available. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-11, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

En bloc consideration of nominations (S.Res. 817): A Senate procedure step: it lets the Senate vote on a large batch of presidential nominations all at once instead of one at a time — executive-branch officials, judges, and ambassadors, including posts at the Departments of Defense, Energy, Interior, State, and Treasury and several boards and commissions. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-03, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (S.J.Res. 181): Orders the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities in or against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending against an attack on itself, its personnel, or its facilities in other countries. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-05-06, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Photo identification requirements for federal elections (S. 5271): Requires voters to show physical photo ID to get a ballot in federal elections. Someone without ID can cast a provisional ballot, but it only counts if they show ID within three days (or swear they lack it for religious reasons). Voting by mail would require sending a copy of a photo ID, or the last four digits of a Social Security number plus a sworn statement that ID couldn't reasonably be obtained. Overseas military voters and certain disabled or elderly voters are exempt, and states must work to make free ID imaging available. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-11, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

En bloc consideration of nominations (S.Res. 817): A Senate procedure step: it lets the Senate vote on a large batch of presidential nominations all at once instead of one at a time — executive-branch officials, judges, and ambassadors, including posts at the Departments of Defense, Energy, Interior, State, and Treasury and several boards and commissions. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-03, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (S.J.Res. 181): Orders the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities in or against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending against an attack on itself, its personnel, or its facilities in other countries. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-05-06, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Photo identification requirements for federal elections (S. 5271): Requires voters to show physical photo ID to get a ballot in federal elections. Someone without ID can cast a provisional ballot, but it only counts if they show ID within three days (or swear they lack it for religious reasons). Voting by mail would require sending a copy of a photo ID, or the last four digits of a Social Security number plus a sworn statement that ID couldn't reasonably be obtained. Overseas military voters and certain disabled or elderly voters are exempt, and states must work to make free ID imaging available. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-11, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

En bloc consideration of nominations (S.Res. 817): A Senate procedure step: it lets the Senate vote on a large batch of presidential nominations all at once instead of one at a time — executive-branch officials, judges, and ambassadors, including posts at the Departments of Defense, Energy, Interior, State, and Treasury and several boards and commissions. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-03, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (S.J.Res. 181): Orders the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities in or against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending against an attack on itself, its personnel, or its facilities in other countries. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-05-06, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Photo identification requirements for federal elections (S. 5271): Requires voters to show physical photo ID to get a ballot in federal elections. Someone without ID can cast a provisional ballot, but it only counts if they show ID within three days (or swear they lack it for religious reasons). Voting by mail would require sending a copy of a photo ID, or the last four digits of a Social Security number plus a sworn statement that ID couldn't reasonably be obtained. Overseas military voters and certain disabled or elderly voters are exempt, and states must work to make free ID imaging available. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-11, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

En bloc consideration of nominations (S.Res. 817): A Senate procedure step: it lets the Senate vote on a large batch of presidential nominations all at once instead of one at a time — executive-branch officials, judges, and ambassadors, including posts at the Departments of Defense, Energy, Interior, State, and Treasury and several boards and commissions. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-03, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (S.J.Res. 181): Orders the President to remove U.S. armed forces from hostilities in or against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending against an attack on itself, its personnel, or its facilities in other countries. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-05-06, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

request.question: What does Teri Ann Hourihan say about ARIZONA?

expectedRecords.quote: Teri Ann Hourihan ARIZONA GOVERNOR, NO LABELS PARTY I AM THE CANDIDATE THAT NO ONE ELSE IS OR IS WILLING TO BE — FOR THE PEOPLE = YOU.
I AM NOT FOR THE SYSTEM THAT FAILS US BUT FOR THE PEOPLE FIRST AND FOREMOST WHO ARE HURTING IN ARIZONA.

As Governor, my loyalty will be to the people of Arizona, not to special interests or big donors.” —Teri Ann Hourihan My Heart is For Arizona I rejected the No Labels Party endorsement because I stand for Arizona and not for a political party!
As Governor of Arizona, I will never take for granted the opportunity to serve the people of this great state.
My focus is simple: creating positive change, restoring accountability, and putting the people of Arizona first.
What I once saw as the darkest season of my life has become a calling to serve Arizona.
My goal is simple: improve the quality of life for every person who calls Arizona home.
November is ahead of us, and together we can save Arizona.
🙌🇺🇸 From the very beginning, I told Arizona, the media, my party, and everyone who would listen that I believe this campaign is a calling on my life.
Now it’s time for Arizona to recognize something important: we are not just a two-party state.
Get excited, Arizona!
As Governor of Arizona, I will not take corporate PAC money, billionaire donations, or special-interest endorsements.
My loyalty will be to the people of Arizona—not to those seeking favors, influence, or access.
Arizona deserves leadership that cannot be bought.
Together, we can build an Arizona that works for all of us Leading Arizona with Truth and Accountability Teri Ann Hourihan for AZ Governor .
Arizona has so much to lose if the wrong leader earns the Governor’s seat.
We can continue down the same path of division, waste, and failed leadership, or we can choose a new direction built on truth, accountability, and putting the people of Arizona first.
Arizona deserves better, and I’m ready to lead FRIENDSHIP AND GRATITUDE Teri Ann Hourihan for AZ Governor.

I regained my voice because his encouragement kept me speaking Q&A Affordability Arizona’s cost of living and inflation rates remain above national targets, making it increasingly difficult for families to afford housing, groceries, transportation, and other necessities.
Arizona’s rapid growth, combined with water shortages, drought conditions, and housing supply constraints, has driven costs higher.
Q&A Healthcare Healthcare costs continue to place a significant burden on Arizona families, employers, and healthcare providers.
Arizona can lead the nation in creating a healthcare system that supports families, employers, providers, and taxpayers while delivering better outcomes for everyone.
As Governor, I will fight for practical, fiscally responsible solutions that lower costs, expand choices, and make healthcare more affordable for every Arizona family.
Meet Teri Teri Ann Hourihan is a proud Arizona native, devoted mother, small business owner of an integrated health care company, and Licensed Professional Counselor (LPC).
Teri entered the race for Governor with one mission: to serve the people of Arizona.

Arizona deserves better.” — Teri Statement Teri chose to run as an Independent/No Labels because she believes the growing political division in our state and nation is preventing meaningful solutions and leaving too many people behind.
She believes Arizona needs leadership that brings people together, not further apart, and that the needs of citizens must always come before political agendas.

Guided by honesty, integrity, accountability, and common sense, Teri is committed to making decisions based on what is best for Arizona—not what is best for political parties, special interests, or wealthy donors.

She believes many of Arizona’s systems are no longer serving citizens as intended and that meaningful reform is necessary to protect families, strengthen communities, and improve quality of life across the state.
She is committed to being accessible, approachable, and accountable to the people of Arizona.
Teri’s Debate on 06/18/2026 Simply put, as Governor I will save Families and Save Arizona!
My mission is to create a government that is truly for the people and not for the government, to expose the truth, and to create a better Arizona for us all to live in.

The CARES Act (March 2020): The first pandemic relief law: $1,200 payments to most adults, expanded unemployment benefits, and forgivable loans to keep small businesses paying staff. The House agreed to the Senate amendment by voice vote on March 27, 2020, so there is no House roll-call position for an individual member. Selection criteria: Major legislation that became law (plus one additional selected proposal), and consequential Senate confirmations, since 2020 — chosen before looking at how anyone voted.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.

request.question: What does Gregory M. Sargent say about State?

expectedRecords.quote: Greg Sargent for NH State Representative | Newbury & New London Why?
I govern from what we love about this state instead.
Public schools even better than the ones we're proud of now, funded by the state, not your local property tax.
My House Committee Assignment House Resources, Recreation & Development Lake protection, state parks, water quality, and land use, including Lake Sunapee and Mt.
Governing out of joy means this: people who work hard should be able to get ahead in this state, and I will vote that way every session.
Supported SB 647, a bipartisan prescription discount program: Up to 80% off generics at every NH pharmacy, at no cost to the state.
Brought state minimum wage bills back to the House floor (HB 1484; HB 442; HB 726).
But "no broad-based tax" has quietly become an excuse for the state to push its own bills down onto your local property tax.
I apply one test to the state budget: does it actually lower the cost of living here, or does it just move the cost around?
The state Supreme Court has repeatedly found this underfunding unconstitutional.
New Hampshire ranks 48th in the country for per-person state aid to cities and towns.

For more than a decade the state has stepped back from its share of local costs: cutting revenue sharing, ending its contribution to the retirement system, and reducing the towns' share of the meals and rooms tax.
Hundreds of millions in state obligations have been shifted onto local property tax bills as a result.
Meanwhile, the state now spends over $50 million a year on a school voucher program that increasingly subsidizes families who never attended public school to begin with.
My Record Voted for the state to meet its constitutional obligation to fund an adequate education (HB 651; HB 1799; HB 1826), the single biggest driver of local property taxes.

What I do support is having large corporations pay more through the Business Profits Tax, and restoring the Interest & Dividends tax only for those earning more than $250,000 a year in interest and dividends income, so the state's bills stop landing on your property taxes.

What Is Next Holding the state to its constitutional duty to fund education so the cost stops landing on local property taxpayers, backing targeted relief for owner-occupied homes, and ending a decade of downshifting, all without an income or sales tax.
The NH Supreme Court agrees: The state must raise per-pupil adequacy funding.
My Record Supported state funding for an adequate education (HB 651; HB 1799; HB 1826).
What Is Next Holding the state to the Supreme Court's adequacy ruling, and keeping public education dollars in public schools.
+ Where I Stand I serve on the House Resources, Recreation & Development Committee, with direct jurisdiction over lake protection, water quality, and state parks.
It creates no new state tax and forces nothing on anyone.
Supported state affordable housing programs (HB 1405; HB 1661), the housing champion program (HB 1196), and Partners in Housing (HB 572).
The Team You Have Two Votes This district elects two State Representatives.

Make Your Plan Voting in Newbury & New London Key Dates State Primary: Tuesday, September 8, 2026 General Election: Tuesday, November 3, 2026 Where to Vote Newbury: Town Office Building, 937 Route 103 New London: Whipple Memorial Town Hall, 25 Seamans Road Polls open 7 a.m.

returnedRecords.text: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (H.R. 6500): A stop-gap spending bill. It keeps the federal government funded — mostly at last year's levels — until December 11, 2026, or until the regular spending bills pass, whichever comes first, preventing a shutdown when the budget year starts October 1. It makes exceptions for programs like WIC food aid, small-business loans, disaster relief, the Indian Health Service, and wildfire fighting, and extends expiring programs covering agriculture, flood insurance, cybersecurity, transportation, veterans benefits, and housing. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-08-12, read at the bill page.

Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (H R 8884): Lets the Social Security Administration restart pilot programs — paused since 2022 — that test changes to disability benefits meant to help people on disability work more without losing income. Joining a pilot is voluntary, a participant's total income can't go down because of it, and the agency must tell Congress about each pilot 120 days before starting it. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-26, read at the bill page.

War Powers resolution on hostilities against Iran (H CON RES 89): Orders the President to pull U.S. armed forces out of hostilities against Iran unless Congress declares war or votes to authorize the use of military force. It says this doesn't stop the U.S. from defending itself, its forces, its diplomatic buildings, or allies from imminent attack. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-04-27, read at the bill page.

Congressional budget for fiscal year 2027 (H CON RES 113): Congress's budget blueprint for 2027 (with targets through 2036). It doesn't spend money itself — it sets the overall numbers for spending, taxes, and debt, and tells four House committees to write follow-up legislation allowed to increase the deficit by set amounts. That follow-up uses a fast-track process the Senate can't filibuster. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-30, read at the bill page.

Stop Insider Trading Act (H R 7008): Bars members of Congress — and their spouses and dependent children — from buying stock in individual companies, and requires public notice 7 to 14 days before they sell stock they already own. Broad investments like widely held funds are exempt. Breaking the rules brings a fine of at least $2,000 or 10% of the trade (plus any profit made), which can't be paid with campaign money. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-07-17, read at the bill page.

National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (H R 8800): The yearly military policy bill. It says what the Department of Defense (and the Energy Department's nuclear-weapons programs) may spend money on for the 2027 budget year — which aircraft and ships to buy, how many people serve in the military, pay and health care rules for troops, how the Pentagon buys things, how it works with other countries, and rules for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Basis: Congressional Research Service summary, version updated 2026-06-29, read at the bill page.
